I've been using Linux as my main desktop and laptop OS for ten years. I haven't dual-booted for five years. I'm also a gamer.

For games, it definitely isn't ready for mass-desktop adoption. Firstly there's the issue of Linux ports; while we have seen an unprecedented increase in the number of developers porting their games to Linux over the past two years, we're still not quite there yet. There still aren't enough triple-A titles making their way to Linux, purely because there's not enough of a return on the investment. I'd like to say Steam OS will change this, but I'm not sure it will; Steam boxes are not going to be competitive in a console-oriented market because they don't perform as well at the same price point, and they're not going to be competitive as an alternative to desktops because 90% of the triple-A titles that run on Windows will not run on them. Secondly, there's the issue of drivers. I haven't used ATI/AMD cards since the early 2000s but I gather their drivers are a bit of a joke; constant rendering and performance issues. Nvidia are much better, but on the same hardware they still don't perform as well as they do on Windows. Linux users running Nvidia cards are such a small percentage of their customer-base that there's very little incentive for them to bring their drivers up to the same standard. There's also the issue that you have to run closed-source blobs to get anywhere near decent performance for both nVidia and AMD, so nobody outside of the respective companies really knows what they're doing. There are open-source alternative drivers maintained by the community, but they perform very poorly. At that point you have to wonder if you're better off sacrificing all your privacy and just running Windows.

My solution is to do most of my triple-A gaming on consoles and run anything that has ports, usually indie stuff, on my Linux box.

For general desktop usage, I think Linux is a viable alternative, but you will have to put in a bit of time to learn how everything works. Unless you're doing video editing and possibly high-level graphics editing then I genuinely don't think there's anything you can do on Windows that you can't do better on Linux. Make sure you're familiar with the concept of package management; all your software should come from central repositories specific to your distro, you don't usually go out and Google executables to download on a Linux-based system. Also, don't settle for the first distro you try. Spend a few hours with several, get it set-up the way you like it, but if there's something you're not happy about that you can't fix yourself then try another distro. I'd definitely recommend Ubuntu, Elementary and Linux Mint, and if you're feeling a bit braver and want to tweak a bit more, try Antergos (which is basically entry-level Arch, although I think their installer might be broken at the moment).

Hope this helps.
